Replace the interval with a prediction for future data
questions.answer: Apply the log transformation to both interval endpoints
questions.explanation: A monotone transformation preserves the probability of an interval event when its endpoints are transformed.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 114, Credible region

questions.clue: Overestimating a parameter costs more per unit than underestimating it. Which posterior summary reflects this asymmetric absolute loss?
choices: A quantile at a probability above one half
The median regardless of the cost ratio
A quantile at a probability below one half
The posterior mode regardless of the cost ratio
questions.answer: A quantile at a probability below one half
questions.explanation: The optimal quantile probability is the underestimation cost divided by the sum of both costs.
questions.reference: Manuel Arellano, CEMFI, Quantile Methods, p. 1, Asymmetric absolute loss. https://www.cemfi.es/~arellano/quantile-methods-notes.pdf

questions.concept: beta prior strength response to data
questions.clue: Two beta priors have the same mean but one has more total prior concentration. Which mean usually moves less after the same Bernoulli data?
choices: The posterior mean under the less concentrated prior
The posterior mean under the more concentrated prior
Both posterior means always move equally
Whichever posterior has more observed successes when both use the same data
Whichever prior has greater variance at that mean
questions.answer: The posterior mean under the more concentrated prior
questions.explanation: Holding the prior mean fixed, larger total beta concentration gives the data less relative weight.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 100, Conjugate prior

questions.clue: Blood pressure is repeatedly measured on each of 40 participants. In a two-level model, what are the groups?
choices: Measurement occasions considered one by one
All readings treated as one group
questions.explanation: Repeated measurements are nested within participants, allowing person-specific effects.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 288, Multilevel models

questions.clue: Hospitals have different treatment effects but identical modeled baselines. Which term needs to vary by hospital?
questions.explanation: The effect is the contrast between treatment levels, represented by the treatment slope.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 354, Random coefficient models

questions.clue: A hierarchical regression models school effects after accounting for school poverty rates. Toward what can a noisy school estimate shrink?
choices: The expected school effect at its poverty rate
The mean of the unrelated response errors
The overall mean of raw school scores in all cases
questions.answer: The expected school effect at its poverty rate
questions.explanation: The group-level regression supplies a conditional target based on the school's predictor.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 288, Multilevel models

questions.clue: For a normal random-intercept model, what happens to the group intercepts as the between-group variance goes to zero?
choices: They collapse to a common intercept
They remain separated by the original group means
They take on the observation variance
questions.answer: They collapse to a common intercept
questions.explanation: A distribution with no between-group variance assigns the same intercept to every group.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance components

questions.clue:
μpost = (wₛ x̄ + wₚ μ)/(wₛ + wₚ)
The weights are sampling precision and prior precision. What quantity does the formula describe?
choices: A marginal prior mean with no data
questions.explanation: With normal sampling and prior distributions, their precisions determine how much each mean contributes.
questions.reference: Duke University STA 601, Lecture 3, The Normal Model and Prior/Posterior Predictive Distributions. https://www2.stat.duke.edu/courses/Fall21/sta601.001/slides/03-normal-predictive-distributions.html
questions.math_clue:
$\mu_{\mathrm{post}}=\frac{w_s\bar{x}+w_p\mu}{w_s+w_p}$
The weights are sampling precision and prior precision. What quantity does the formula describe?

questions.clue: Students are nested in schools. Which candidate is naturally a school-level predictor?
questions.explanation: School budget is shared by the students grouped in that institution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 288, Multilevel models

questions.clue: Each clinician treats patients at several clinics, and each clinic has several clinicians. Which random-intercept structure fits these associations?
choices: A common intercept with no group effects
questions.explanation: The levels overlap in both directions, so neither grouping factor uniquely contains the other.
questions.reference: Bates et al., Fitting Linear Mixed-Effects Models Using lme4, Multiple random-effects terms. https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/lme4/vignettes/lmer.pdf

questions.clue: Before seeing outcomes a model treats school effects as exchangeable given the same school-level covariates. What change leaves their joint prior unchanged?
choices: Force the effects to be equal
Permute labels among schools with matching covariates
Replace the hyperprior with a point mass
questions.answer: Permute labels among schools with matching covariates
questions.explanation: Conditional exchangeability means relabeling otherwise comparable groups leaves the joint distribution unchanged.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 155, Exchangeability

questions.clue: A predictive simulation generates two outcomes for patients in the same new hospital. How should their simulated hospital effects be related?
choices: Draw a different hospital effect for each patient
Reuse the effect for a different observed hospital in each outcome
Give one patient a new hospital effect and omit it for the other
Replace both hospital effects with independent residuals
Use the same new hospital effect for both outcomes
questions.answer: Use the same new hospital effect for both outcomes
questions.explanation: Patients in the same simulated hospital share one hospital effect while their individual residuals can differ.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, Model checking and improvement. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/bayescomputation/bdachapter6.pdf

questions.clue: For a random-intercept model with independent residuals, what causes outcomes from the same group to be correlated marginally?
choices: A fixed intercept shared by all records
questions.explanation: The same random shift appears in both outcomes, inducing covariance when averaged over that shift.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 221, Intraclass correlation

questions.clue:
Var(Yᵢⱼ given fixed covariates) = τ² + σ²
What does the variance sum represent in an independent random-intercept model?
choices: Within-group variance conditional on the group effect
Covariance of outcomes in two independent groups
Marginal variance of one outcome after averaging over the group effect
Variance of the group effect alone
The standard error of the fixed intercept
questions.answer: Marginal variance of one outcome after averaging over the group effect
questions.explanation: A single outcome receives both the group-level random shift and individual residual noise.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance components
questions.math_clue:
$\operatorname{Var}(Y_{ij}\mid\mathrm{fixed\ covariates})=\tau^2+\sigma^2$
What does the variance sum represent in an independent random-intercept model?

questions.clue: A clinic effect has prior N(μ, τ²). Which feature of this model controls spread across clinic effects?
choices: Prior centre of the clinic-level effects
Estimated effect of the first clinic
questions.explanation: The variance parameter of the shared prior governs how widely clinic-level effects vary around the common centre.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 211, Hyperparameter
questions.math_clue: A clinic effect has prior $N(\mu,\tau^2)$. Which feature of this model controls spread across clinic effects?

questions.clue: Two otherwise identical hierarchical fits differ only in their assumed between-group variance. Which fit tends to leave group estimates closer to their unpooled means?
choices: The one with exactly zero between-group variance
The one imposing one common group intercept
The one with more between-group variance
The one with less between-group variance
questions.answer: The one with more between-group variance
questions.explanation: A broader group distribution tolerates larger true differences, so it pulls the group estimates less strongly toward its center.
questions.reference: Duke University STA 601, Lecture 3, The Normal Model and Prior/Posterior Predictive Distributions. https://www2.stat.duke.edu/courses/Fall21/sta601.001/slides/03-normal-predictive-distributions.html

questions.clue: When comparing observed and replicated minima in a posterior predictive check, why usually keep the replicate sample size fixed to the observed size?
choices: Replicate size changes the observed minimum retrospectively
The distribution of a sample minimum depends on the number of observations
Posterior samples must always equal the observed sample size
A fixed size makes every replicated minimum identical
Using the same size makes the underlying model true
questions.answer: The distribution of a sample minimum depends on the number of observations
questions.explanation: The more observations in a replicate, the greater the chance it contains an unusually small value.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, Model checking and improvement. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/bayescomputation/bdachapter6.pdf

questions.clue: A model gets the overall spread right but misses the pattern across time. Which check would expose that specific mismatch?
choices: Compare the width of the prior to its median
Compare posterior mean and mode of the variance
Compare time-ordered residual autocorrelation to replications
Compare simulated and observed sample size
questions.answer: Compare time-ordered residual autocorrelation to replications
questions.explanation: A discrepancy that preserves time ordering can detect serial dependence hidden by overall spread.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, Model checking and improvement. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/bayescomputation/bdachapter6.pdf

questions.clue: An observed mean is typical of replicated means, but the observed minimum is far below all the replicated minima. What conclusion is justified?
choices: The model captures the mean better than the lower tail
The model captures both features equally well
The model gives an exact out-of-sample error estimate
The model captures the lower tail better than the mean
The posterior must have used an improper prior
questions.answer: The model captures the mean better than the lower tail
questions.explanation: Different discrepancies probe different aspects, and the minimum points to the tail failure.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, Model checking and improvement. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/bayescomputation/bdachapter6.pdf

questions.clue:
P(Trep ≥ Tobs given y)
What does this posterior predictive check summarize?
choices: The share of observations included in the model fit
The share of replicated discrepancies at least as large as observed
The share of prior parameter draws above their posterior mean
The chance of a smaller discrepancy under the prior
A posterior probability that the entire model is true
questions.answer: The share of replicated discrepancies at least as large as observed
questions.explanation: The upper-tail check compares the observed discrepancy against discrepancies from replicated datasets.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, Model checking and improvement. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/bayescomputation/bdachapter6.pdf
questions.math_clue:
$P(T_{\mathrm{rep}}\geq T_{\mathrm{obs}}\mid y)$
What does this posterior predictive check summarize?

questions.clue: The target is sales four weeks ahead. Which forecast errors should validate that target?
choices: Errors from one-week-ahead forecasts using all weeks
Residuals fitted to the full sales series
Errors from four-week-ahead forecasts made using only data then available
Errors from fitting a model to each forecasted observation
Errors from forecasts made with future covariates unavailable in practice
questions.answer: Errors from four-week-ahead forecasts made using only data then available
questions.explanation: Validation should match the planned forecast horizon and information available when predicting.
questions.reference: Stan User’s Guide, Held-Out Evaluation and Cross-Validation. https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_36/stan-users-guide/cross-validation.html

questions.clue: Two candidate models use improper priors with arbitrary multiplicative constants. What goes wrong with a Bayes factor formed directly from their marginal likelihoods?
choices: It becomes the ratio of posterior modes
It is determined by the held-out log score instead
It can depend on the arbitrary constants
It is unchanged because all such constants cancel across models
questions.answer: It can depend on the arbitrary constants
questions.explanation: An arbitrary prior scaling carries through to model evidence and can alter its ratio.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, Model checking and improvement. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/bayescomputation/bdachapter6.pdf

questions.clue: Two candidate models make different forecasts, and neither has overwhelming posterior support. What does Bayesian model averaging account for by keeping both forecasts?
choices: A lack of uncertainty within each model
Uncertainty about which candidate model to use
A need to estimate all prior probabilities from the held-out cases
A guarantee that both models are correct
questions.answer: Uncertainty about which candidate model to use
questions.explanation: Averaging can carry uncertainty about the model choice into the combined predictive distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 38, Bayesian model averaging

questions.clue:
Σᵢ Varposterior[log p(yᵢ∣θ)]
What variation gives this WAIC complexity term?
choices: Variation across data points at one fixed parameter value
Variation across posterior parameter draws within each data contribution
Variation across prior draws without using data
Variation across sample sizes for a fixed observed point
Variation across models with no parameter draws
questions.answer: Variation across posterior parameter draws within each data contribution
questions.explanation: Each observation contributes posterior variability in its log-likelihood, and those pointwise variances are added.
questions.reference: Gelman, Hwang and Vehtari, Understanding predictive information criteria for Bayesian models, §3.4, WAIC. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf
questions.math_clue:
$\sum_i\operatorname{Var}_{\mathrm{post}}\left[\log p(y_i\mid\theta)\right]$
What variation gives this WAIC complexity term?

questions.clue: A few importance weights dominate a leave-one-out approximation, and the estimated Pareto shape is large. What should this flag?
choices: A missing likelihood normalization constant in all models
An exact refit for the affected case
An unreliable approximation for the affected held-out case
Overly narrow priors in every parameter
questions.answer: An unreliable approximation for the affected held-out case
questions.explanation: A heavy upper tail of importance weights makes the approximate held-out prediction unstable.
questions.reference: Vehtari, Gelman and Gabry, Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/loo_stan.pdf

questions.clue: What does each model average over to obtain the marginal likelihood used in a Bayes factor?
choices: Its prior over its own unknown parameters
Its posterior over its own unknown parameters
Its sampling distribution over all possible datasets
The priors of the other candidate models
questions.answer: Its prior over its own unknown parameters
questions.explanation: Marginal likelihood averages the likelihood of the observed data over possible parameters weighted by that model’s prior.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 37, Bayes factor

questions.clue: A multilevel model will predict new patients at the same hospitals used in training. Which holdout best mimics this use?
choices: Fit to the held-out patient before scoring that patient
Score all patients used for fitting
Hold out hospitals based on their true outcome rates
Hold out patients within hospitals while retaining other patients at those hospitals
Hold out every patient from selected hospitals
questions.answer: Hold out patients within hospitals while retaining other patients at those hospitals
questions.explanation: Within-hospital holdouts preserve the hospital context that will be available in deployment.
questions.reference: Stan User’s Guide, Held-Out Evaluation and Cross-Validation. https://mc-stan.org/docs/2_36/stan-users-guide/cross-validation.html

questions.clue:
D(θ̄) + 2 pD
D is deviance, θ̄ is the posterior mean, and pD is an effective parameter count. Which criterion has this form?
questions.explanation: This DIC form adds a complexity correction to the deviance evaluated at the posterior mean.
questions.reference: Gelman, Hwang and Vehtari, Understanding predictive information criteria for Bayesian models, §3.3, DIC. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/waic_understand3.pdf
questions.math_clue:
$D(\bar{\theta})+2p_D$
$D$ is deviance, $\bar{\theta}$ is the posterior mean, and $p_D$ is an effective parameter count. Which criterion has this form?

questions.concept: why different stacking and bma weights
questions.clue: Which property lets predictive stacking give different model weights from Bayesian model averaging on the same data?
choices: Stacking always uses each model’s posterior probability
Stacking can compare only nested models
Stacking optimizes a score for the held-out predictions of a mixture
Stacking disregards the component predictive distributions
Stacking chooses weights before any observations are available
questions.answer: Stacking optimizes a score for the held-out predictions of a mixture
questions.explanation: The stacking target is predictive performance of the combined distribution rather than a posterior allocation of model probability.
questions.reference: Yao et al., Using Stacking to Average Bayesian Predictive Distributions. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/stacking.pdf

questions.clue: Before fitting a time-to-event model, simulations often generate impossible negative event times. What is the first component to reconsider?
choices: The numbers in a posterior predictive check
The fold-level calculation of log scores
The prior and sampling model together
questions.answer: The prior and sampling model together
questions.explanation: These failures occur before the data are used, so they arise from the assumptions of the prior predictive model.
questions.reference: Gelman et al., Bayesian Data Analysis, 3rd ed., Ch. 6, Model checking and improvement. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/bayescomputation/bdachapter6.pdf

questions.clue: Model A places higher probability on held-out observations than model B under the same log score. What did the comparison directly favor?
choices: The assumption that A has no bad residual patterns
A’s parameter estimates for every scientific question
The claim that A is the true data-generating process
A larger prior probability for A
A’s held-out predictive accuracy under that score
questions.answer: A’s held-out predictive accuracy under that score
questions.explanation: Held-out log score measures scored prediction of the held-out data.
questions.reference: Vehtari, Gelman and Gabry, Practical Bayesian model evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. https://sites.stat.columbia.edu/gelman/research/published/loo_stan.pdf
